summary: Working in linguistics and history/archaeology, John Crawfurd studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh (~1800–1803). He served as a physician for the East India Company (1803–1808) and succeeded Stamford Raffles in 1823.

John D. Dunne, a scholar of Buddhist studies, philosophy, and Tibetology, earned his Ph.D. at Harvard under Masatoshi Nagatomi and Malcolm David Eckel. He taught at Emory (~2005–2016) and held a Distinguished Chair at UW–Madison (1999).

John D. Kelly is a scholar in Indology and religious studies. He has been affiliated with the University of Chicago (attested 2007, 2026), where he serves as Christian W. Mackauer Professor of Anthropology and of Social Sciences.

Working in Indology and linguistics, John D. Smith was a Lecturer in Sanskrit at SOAS University of London (1975). He later joined the University of Cambridge as University Lecturer in Sanskrit (1984) and served as Professor (2001–2007).

John Daido Loori worked in Buddhist and religious studies, studying at Rutgers and under Soen Nakagawa and Hakuyu Taizan Maezumi. After a 1974 post at Naropa University, he served as Abbot of Zen Mountain Monastery (~1980–2009).
Active in Buddhist and religious studies, John Daishin Buksbazen studied at the Zen Center of Los Angeles under Hakuyu Taizan Maezumi, Bernie Glassman, and Wendy Egyoku Nakao (all attested 2002).

Philosopher John Dewey studied at the University of Vermont (~1875–1879) and Johns Hopkins (~1882–1884). He held posts at the universities of Michigan (~1884–1894), Minnesota (~1888–1889), Chicago (~1894–1904), and Columbia (~1904–1930).

John Dowson was an Indologist and linguist who studied under Edwin Norris. He served as a tutor at East India Company College (~1855–1858) and as Professor of Hindustani at University College London and Staff College, Camberley (1855–1877).

John E. Cort works in Indology and religious studies. He studied at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (~1970–1974) and Harvard University (~1980–1984), and he became a professor at Denison University (~1993).

Working in history, archaeology, and Indology, John F. Richards studied at the University of New Hampshire (~1957–1961) and UC Berkeley (~1961–1970). He held posts at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (~1968–1977) and Duke University (~1977–2007).

John Faithfull Fleet, an Indology and history/archaeology scholar, studied at University College London (~1865–1867). He served in the Indian Civil Service (1865–1897), Bombay Civil Service (~1867–1897), and as Epigraphist to the Government of India (1883–1886).
John Firminger Duthie served as Superintendent of the Botanical Gardens, Saharanpur (~1876–1903) and as Director of the Botanical Survey of India (~1891–1903).

John George Woodroffe was an Indology and religious studies scholar who studied at University College, Oxford (~1884–1888). He was a Calcutta High Court Judge (~1904–1922) and Reader in Indian Law at Oxford (~1923–1930).

John Gombojab Hangin worked in linguistics and Iranian/Central Asian studies, earning degrees from Columbia (-1963) and Indiana University (~1965–1970). After posts at Johns Hopkins and Georgetown, he was a full professor at Indiana (1965–1989).
John Griffiths was an Indologist and historian/archaeologist who studied at the Royal College of Art. He held a post at the Sir Jamsetjee Jeejebhoy School of Art from ~1865 to 1895.
John Hallett Batten was active in the fields of history, archaeology, and Indology. He completed his studies at Charterhouse School (~1823–1827) and the East India Company College (~1827–1829).

John Henry Hutton was an Indologist and historian/archaeologist who studied at Chigwell School (~1898–1904) and Worcester College, Oxford (~1904–1908). He served in the Indian Civil Service from ~1909 to 1936.

Classicist John Henry Wright studied at Dartmouth and Leipzig under Georg Curtius. He held posts at Ohio State (1873–1876), Dartmouth (1878–1886), and Johns Hopkins (1886), before serving as Professor at Harvard University (~1887–1908).

An Indologist, John Herbert Harington served as secretary (1790) and president (1825–1828) of The Asiatic Society. He was also an honorary professor of British government laws and regulations at Fort William College (~1801–1823).

John Hick worked in philosophy and religious studies, studying at Edinburgh (~1945–1948) and Oxford (~1948–1950). He held posts at Cornell, Princeton Seminary, Cambridge, the University of Birmingham (~1967–1982), and Claremont Graduate University (~1979–1993).
